scenarios.context: An interviewer asks a candidate about her experience.

speakerA.en: Thank you for coming. Could you start by telling us a little about your background?
What attracted you to this position?
Can you describe a situation in which you had to solve a difficult problem at work?
That sounds stressful. How do you usually handle pressure?
What would you say is your greatest weakness?
Where do you see yourself in five years' time?

speakerB.en: Certainly. I graduated three years ago and have worked as a junior accountant, mainly dealing with invoices and monthly reports.
The company has an excellent reputation, and the role would let me take on more responsibility and develop my skills.
Last year, we discovered an error in a client's accounts just before a deadline. I stayed late, found the cause and corrected it with my manager.
I prioritise the most urgent tasks, communicate clearly with my colleagues and take short breaks to stay focused.
I sometimes spend too long perfecting small details, but I'm learning to set time limits for each task.
I hope to be a senior member of the team, perhaps leading a small group and mentoring new employees.

scenarios.context: A new employee goes through a contract with the HR manager.

speakerA.en: Before you sign, let me go through the main points of your contract. Please stop me if anything is unclear.
Thirty-eight hours, from Monday to Friday. Overtime is paid at one and a half times your normal rate.
Twenty-five days of paid leave, plus public holidays. You need to request time off at least two weeks in advance.
You must inform your manager as early as possible. After three days, you need a doctor's note.
During that time, either side can end the contract with a shorter notice period. After that, the notice period is two months.
Yes, the company contributes to a pension scheme, and you'll also be covered by our health insurance.

speakerB.en: Thank you. First, how many hours per week am I expected to work?
What about holidays? How many days am I entitled to each year?
And what happens if I'm ill and can't come to work?
I noticed a probation period of six months. What does that mean in practice?
I see. Are there any benefits besides the salary, such as a pension plan?
That sounds fair. May I take the contract home and read it carefully before I sign?

scenarios.context: A new employee asks a colleague about deductions from her salary.

speakerA.en: Could you help me understand my payslip? I can't work out why the amount I received is lower than my salary.
What exactly is deducted?
So I don't have to pay the tax myself?
How do I know whether I've paid too much?
That's useful. Is there someone who can help if I get confused?
I'll do some research this weekend, then. Thank you for your patience.

speakerB.en: Of course. The gross salary is what you earn before deductions, and the net salary is what you actually receive.
Income tax, and also contributions to social security and sometimes a pension. These are taken directly by the employer.
Not usually, but you may have to submit a tax return once a year, especially if you have other sources of income.
If you've overpaid, you can claim a refund, so it's important to keep your documents and receipts.
Yes, the tax office has a helpline, and many people use an accountant for their first return.
No problem. Just keep every payslip and your tax number somewhere safe.

scenarios.context: Two colleagues resolve a misunderstanding about a report.

speakerA.en: Can I have a word? I feel that there's been a misunderstanding about who was responsible for the report.
I did include it, but I forgot to mention your name in the final document, and I apologise for that.
Let's agree to communicate more openly from now on. If either of us has a problem, we'll talk about it immediately.
Good idea. We could write down who is responsible for each task and when it's due.
Shall we correct the document and send it to her together?
Perfect. I'm glad we sorted this out calmly.

speakerB.en: Of course. To be honest, I was upset because I thought that you hadn't included my part of the work.
Thank you for being honest. I should have asked you directly instead of complaining to others.
That sounds sensible. I also think we need to clarify our roles at the beginning of each project.
Then there would be no confusion, and our manager would see how we share the workload.
Yes, I'll add my name and the missing paragraph, and you can check the final version.
So am I. It's much better than letting the tension grow.

scenarios.context: An employee tells her manager that she is leaving.

speakerA.en: Do you have a minute? There's something important I'd like to discuss with you.
I've been offered a position in another city, and after careful thought, I've decided to accept it.
My contract requires two months' notice, so my last day would be at the end of January.
Certainly. I'd like to leave everything in good order and hand over my projects properly.
Yes, I'll send an email this afternoon. May I also ask for a reference letter?
That means a lot. I've learnt so much here, and I'm grateful for the opportunities.

speakerB.en: Of course. Please sit down. Is everything all right?
I'm sorry to hear that, but I appreciate you telling me in person. When would you like to leave?
Understood. Would you be willing to help us train your replacement before you go?
Thank you. Could you please put your resignation in writing so that I can forward it to the HR department?
Absolutely. You've been a valuable member of the team, and I'll be happy to recommend you.
We wish you every success, and the door will always be open if you ever want to return.
